question: According to the manual, what is the most important reason for completing a vehicle inspection?
choice_b: To keep the vehicle looking clean for the motor carrier
choice_c: To avoid getting a ticket from a roadside inspector
explanation: The manual states safety is the most important reason for completing a vehicle inspection, since a defect found early could prevent a breakdown or crash.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.1, Why Inspect

question: If a federal or state inspector judges a commercial vehicle to be unsafe, what will they do?
choice_a: Put the vehicle 'out of service' until it is repaired
choice_c: Issue a warning letter to the motor carrier only
choice_d: Suspend the driver's CDL for 30 days
explanation: The manual states that if inspectors judge a vehicle unsafe, they will put it 'out of service' until it is repaired.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.1, Why Inspect

question: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on the front tires of a commercial vehicle?
explanation: The manual specifies at least 4/32-inch tread depth is required in every major groove on front tires, while other tires require only 2/32-inch.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Tire Problems)

question: What type of tires are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus?
explanation: The manual states that regrooved, recapped or retreaded tires on the front wheels of a bus are prohibited.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Tire Problems)

question: What might rust around wheel/lug nuts indicate during an inspection?
choice_a: The tire pressure is too high
choice_c: The nuts may be loose and should be checked for tightness
choice_d: The vehicle needs an oil change
explanation: The manual warns that rust around wheel/lug nuts may mean the nuts are loose, so the driver should check tightness, and re-check a short while after a tire has been changed.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Wheel and Rim Problems)

question: What amount of missing leaf spring material will put a vehicle 'out of service'?
explanation: The manual states that if one-fourth or more of the leaves in a leaf spring are missing or broken, the vehicle will be put 'out of service,' though any defect could be dangerous.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Suspension System Defects)

question: During an inspection, brake shoes or pads worn to less than what thickness are considered a defect?
explanation: The manual lists shoes worn to less than 1/4 inch, missing or broken, as a bad brake drum or shoe defect to look for.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Bad Brake Drums or Shoes)

question: Why can a broken exhaust system be especially dangerous?
choice_a: It can cause the tires to wear unevenly
choice_b: It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_d: It can cause the vehicle to overheat
explanation: The manual explains that a broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Exhaust System Defects)

question: How much steering wheel play can make a vehicle hard to steer?
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make it hard to steer.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Steering System Defects)

question: During the walk-around inspection, why must a driver grab the steering mechanism at the front of the vehicle?
choice_d: To test for looseness in the steering system
explanation: During the Front section of Step 5, the manual instructs the driver to grab the steering mechanism to test for looseness.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 5, Front)

question: Which of the following is listed as required emergency equipment for a commercial vehicle?
choice_d: Warning devices for parked vehicles, such as three reflective warning triangles
explanation: The manual lists warning devices for parked vehicles, for example three reflective warning triangles, six fuses or three liquid burning flares, as required emergency equipment.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Emergency Equipment)

question: When are spare electrical fuses NOT required as part of a vehicle's emergency equipment?
choice_a: When the vehicle is a bus rather than a truck
choice_b: When the vehicle has an automatic transmission
choice_c: When the vehicle is less than one year old
choice_d: When the vehicle is equipped with circuit breakers
explanation: The manual notes spare electrical fuses are required 'unless equipped with circuit breakers.'
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.3, What to Look For (Emergency Equipment)

question: In Step 1 of the seven-step inspection method, what should the driver review?
choice_b: The route map for the trip
choice_c: The fuel receipts from the last fill-up
explanation: Step 1, Vehicle Overview, instructs the driver to review the last vehicle inspection report.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 1)

question: During Step 3 (starting the engine and checking gauges), the air pressure gauge on an air brake system should build from 50 to 90 psi within what time?
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within three minutes, building to the governor cut-out, usually around 120-140 psi.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 3, Look at the Gauges)

question: If the ABS indicator light on the dash stays on after starting the engine rather than turning off, what does this mean?
choice_b: The ABS is not working properly
explanation: The manual states the ABS light should come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 3)

question: How should a driver test hydraulic brakes for leaks during Step 7 of the pre-trip inspection?
choice_a: Drive at highway speed and slam on the brakes
choice_b: Listen for a hissing sound near the wheels
choice_c: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold for five seconds to see if the pedal moves
choice_d: Check the brake fluid color only
explanation: The manual instructs pumping the brake pedal three times, then applying firm pressure and holding for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 7, Test for Hydraulic Leaks)

question: When testing the service brake stopping action in Step 7, at approximately what speed should the driver test the brakes?
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to go about 5 mph and then push the brake pedal firmly to test for pulling or delayed stopping action.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 7, Test Service Brake Stopping Action)

question: During normal operation, what is the expected engine oil pressure range according to Figure 2.5 in the manual?
explanation: Figure 2.5 shows operating oil pressure should be 35-75 PSI, while idling oil pressure is 5-20 PSI.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Figure 2.5, Oil Pressure)

question: What should a driver do if the oil pressure gauge reads low, dropping or fluctuating?
choice_a: Turn on the four-way flashers and reduce speed by half
choice_c: Continue driving carefully to the next rest stop
choice_d: Stop immediately, because without oil the engine can be destroyed rapidly
explanation: Figure 2.5 warns that low, dropping or fluctuating oil pressure means the driver should stop immediately, since without oil the engine can be destroyed rapidly.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Figure 2.5, Oil Pressure)

question: In Step 2 of the pre-trip inspection, before raising the hood or tilting the cab, what should the driver first confirm?
choice_a: That the trailer brakes are released
choice_b: That the fuel tank is full
choice_d: That the parking brakes are on and/or wheels are chocked
explanation: Step 2 begins with 'Check That the Parking Brakes Are On and/or Wheels Chocked' before checking the engine compartment.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.5, Seven-step Inspection Method (Step 2)

topic: Inspection During and After a Trip
question: According to the manual, drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo must inspect the securement of the cargo within the first 50 miles of a trip and every how many miles or hours after that (whichever comes first)?
explanation: The manual states cargo securement must be inspected within the first 50 miles of a trip and every 150 miles or every three hours after, whichever comes first.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.6, Inspection During a Trip

topic: Inspection During and After a Trip
question: What is the purpose of the after-trip inspection report?
choice_a: It is submitted only if the vehicle was involved in a crash
choice_b: It replaces the need for a pre-trip inspection the next day
choice_c: It helps the motor carrier know when the vehicle needs repairs
choice_d: It is used to calculate the driver's pay
explanation: The manual explains the after-trip inspection report, listing any problems found, helps a motor carrier know when the vehicle needs repairs.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.1.2, Types of Vehicle Inspection (After-trip Inspection and Report)

question: What are the four skills listed as required for safe operation of a commercial vehicle in the Basic Control section?
choice_c: Accelerating, steering, stopping and backing safely
explanation: The manual lists accelerating, steering, stopping and backing safely as the skills required for safe operation of a commercial vehicle.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.2, Basic Control of Your Vehicle

question: What should a driver with a manual transmission do to avoid rolling back when starting on an incline?
choice_a: Partly engage the clutch before taking the right foot off the brake
choice_b: Release the parking brake immediately, then apply the accelerator
choice_c: Rev the engine as high as possible before releasing the brake
choice_d: Shift directly into the highest gear
explanation: The manual instructs drivers with manual transmissions to partly engage the clutch before taking their right foot off the brake to avoid rolling back.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.2.1, Accelerating

question: How should a driver hold the steering wheel according to the manual?
choice_a: Firmly with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_b: Loosely, to allow the wheel to self-correct
choice_c: With both hands at the bottom of the wheel
choice_d: With one hand on top and the other resting on the leg
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides, so the wheel does not pull away from their hands if they hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.2.2, Steering

question: Which direction does the manual recommend backing and turning toward whenever possible?
choice_a: Either side, as it makes no difference
choice_b: The passenger's side, because it is closer to the curb
choice_c: The driver's side, so the driver can see better
choice_d: Straight back only, avoiding any turning
explanation: The manual states drivers should back and turn toward the driver's side whenever possible because it allows them to see better, and backing toward the right side is very dangerous.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.2.4, Backing Safely

question: What gear should a driver use when backing, according to the manual?
choice_a: Second gear forward, then releasing the clutch
choice_c: The lowest reverse gear, to correct steering errors more easily
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to always back as slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear so steering errors can be corrected more easily and the vehicle can stop quickly if necessary.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.2.4, Backing Safely (Back Slowly)

question: What technique do most heavy vehicles with manual transmissions require to change gears?
choice_b: Floating gears without using the clutch
explanation: The manual states most heavy vehicles with manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.3.1, Manual Transmissions

question: Before starting down a hill, what should a driver do regarding gear selection?
choice_a: Slow down and shift down to a speed that can be controlled without using the brakes hard
choice_b: Shift into the highest available gear to increase speed
choice_c: Shift into neutral to coast down
choice_d: Keep the same gear used to climb the hill
explanation: The manual advises slowing down and downshifting before starting down a hill so brakes don't have to be used hard and overheat, usually using a lower gear than the one required to climb the same hill.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.3.1, Manual Transmissions (Before Starting Down a Hill)

question: How do multi-speed rear axles and auxiliary transmissions typically get controlled?
choice_a: By a foot pedal separate from the clutch
choice_b: By a selector knob or switch on the gearshift lever of the main transmission
choice_c: By a lever located on the dashboard only
explanation: The manual explains multi-speed rear axles and auxiliary transmissions are usually controlled by a selector knob or switch on the gearshift lever of the main transmission.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.3.2, Multi-speed Rear Axles and Auxiliary Transmissions

question: How many basic types of retarders does the manual list?
explanation: The manual lists four basic types of retarders: exhaust, engine, hydraulic and electric.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.3.4, Retarders

question: Why should a driver turn off the retarder when the road is wet, icy or snow covered?
choice_a: Because retarders damage the tires in wet conditions
choice_b: Because retarders only work above 40 mph
choice_c: Because the retarder may cause the drive wheels to skid when traction is poor
choice_d: Because the retarder will drain the battery in cold weather
explanation: The manual cautions that when drive wheels have poor traction, the retarder may cause them to skid, so it should be turned off on wet, icy or snow-covered roads.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.3.4, Retarders

question: How far ahead does the manual recommend most good drivers look?
explanation: The manual states most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block at lower speeds and about one-quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.4.1, Seeing Ahead

question: At highway speeds, looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead corresponds to approximately what distance?
explanation: The manual states that at highway speeds, 12 to 15 seconds is about one-quarter of a mile, while at lower speeds it is about one block.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.4.1, Seeing Ahead

question: When can mirror adjustment be checked accurately, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only when the trailer(s) are straight
choice_c: Only after the engine has warmed up
choice_d: Only while the vehicle is in motion
explanation: The manual states mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.4.2, Seeing to the Side and Rear (Mirror Adjustment)

question: What is a key characteristic of convex ('fisheye' or 'bugeye') mirrors that a driver must account for?
choice_a: They cannot be adjusted once installed
choice_c: Everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is
choice_d: They only show what is directly behind the vehicle
explanation: The manual explains that in a convex mirror, everything appears smaller than it would look directly, and things also seem farther away than they really are, so drivers must allow for this.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.4.2, Seeing to the Side and Rear (How to Use Mirrors)

question: What are the three rules for using turn signals listed in the manual?
choice_a: Signal loudly, signal briefly, and signal twice
choice_b: Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal
choice_c: Signal after braking, signal while turning, and signal after completing the turn
choice_d: Signal once, signal quietly, and never cancel the signal
explanation: The manual lists three rules for turn signals: signal early, signal continuously (do not cancel until the turn is complete), and cancel your signal after turning.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.1, Signal Your Intentions (Turns)

question: According to the manual, why should a driver never try to direct traffic by signaling other drivers when it is safe to pass?
choice_a: It is illegal in every state without exception
choice_c: It confuses the vehicle's own turn signal system
choice_d: It could cause an accident and the driver could be blamed and liable for costs
explanation: The manual warns that signaling others when it is safe to pass could cause an accident, and the driver could be blamed and it could cost thousands of dollars.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.1, Signal Your Intentions (Do Not Direct Traffic)

question: What should a driver do to warn following drivers before slowing down, according to the manual?
choice_a: Give a few light taps on the brake pedal to flash the brake lights
explanation: The manual recommends a few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, to warn following drivers of the need to slow down.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.1, Signal Your Intentions (Slowing Down)

question: If a driver must stop on the road or shoulder, within how many minutes must emergency warning devices be put out?
explanation: The manual states that if you must stop on the road or shoulder of any road, you must put out your emergency warning devices within 10 minutes.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.2, Communicating Your Presence (When Parked at the Side of the Road)

question: If stopped on a one-way or divided highway, at what distances should warning devices be placed toward the approaching traffic?
explanation: The manual states that on a one-way or divided highway, warning devices should be placed 10 feet, 100 feet and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.2, Communicating Your Presence (When Parked at the Side of the Road)

question: On a two-lane road carrying traffic in both directions, how far behind a hill, curve or other obstruction should the rear-most warning device be placed if visibility is blocked?
explanation: The manual instructs placing a warning device back beyond any hill, curve or other obstruction that prevents other drivers from seeing the vehicle within 500 feet.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.5.2, Communicating Your Presence (When Parked at the Side of the Road)

question: What is the average perception time for an alert driver, according to the manual?
explanation: The manual states the average perception time for an alert driver is 1 3/4 seconds, which accounts for 142 feet traveled at 55 mph.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.1, Stopping Distance (Perception Distance)

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, approximately how far is the braking distance?
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, braking distance can take about 216 feet.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.1, Stopping Distance (Braking Distance)

question: At 55 mph, what is the total minimum stopping distance combining perception, reaction and braking distance?
explanation: The manual states at 55 mph, a vehicle will travel a minimum total stopping distance of 419 feet, combining perception distance, reaction distance and braking distance.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.1, Stopping Distance (Total Stopping Distance)

question: If you triple your speed from 20 to 60 mph, how much greater does the impact and braking distance become?
explanation: The manual states that tripling speed from 20 to 60 mph makes the impact and braking distance nine times greater; doubling speed from 20 to 40 mph makes it four times greater.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.1, Stopping Distance (The Effect of Speed on Stopping Distance)

question: Why do empty trucks require greater stopping distances than fully loaded trucks?
choice_b: An empty vehicle has less traction
choice_c: Empty trucks have weaker brakes installed by manufacturers
choice_d: Empty trucks travel faster on average
explanation: The manual explains that brakes, tires, springs and shock absorbers on heavy vehicles are designed to work best when fully loaded, and empty trucks require greater stopping distances because an empty vehicle has less traction.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.1, Stopping Distance (The Effect of Vehicle Weight on Stopping Distance)

question: On a wet road, the manual recommends reducing speed by about how much compared to dry-road speed?
explanation: The manual recommends reducing speed by about one-third on a wet road, for example slowing from 55 to about 35 mph.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.2, Matching Speed to the Road Surface (Slippery Surfaces)

question: What is 'black ice' according to the manual?
choice_a: Ice that has turned dark from road dirt
choice_b: A thin, clear layer of ice that lets the road show through, making it look wet
choice_d: Ice that only forms in shaded areas
explanation: The manual describes black ice as a thin layer that is clear enough that you can see the road underneath it, making the road look wet.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.2, Matching Speed to the Road Surface (Identifying Slippery Surfaces)

question: According to the manual, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as what, if there is a lot of water on the road?
explanation: The manual states hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water, and it is more likely with low tire pressure or worn tread.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.2, Matching Speed to the Road Surface (Hydroplaning)

question: If a vehicle begins to hydroplane, what does the manual say a driver should do?
choice_a: Release the accelerator and push in the clutch to let the wheels turn freely
choice_b: Brake hard immediately to slow down
choice_c: Accelerate to power through the water
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel sharply to regain traction
explanation: The manual instructs that if the vehicle is hydroplaning, you can regain control by releasing the accelerator and pushing in the clutch, and should not use the brakes to slow down.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.2, Matching Speed to the Road Surface (Hydroplaning)

question: What has testing shown about trucks with a high center of gravity taking a curve at the posted speed limit?
choice_a: They cannot roll over if the driver brakes while turning
choice_b: They can roll over even at the posted speed limit for the curve
choice_c: They only roll over above twice the posted limit
choice_d: They are completely safe at any posted speed limit
explanation: The manual states tests have shown that trucks with a high center of gravity can roll over at the posted speed limit for a curve.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.3, Speed and Curves

question: Why is braking while in a curve considered dangerous?
choice_b: It confuses other drivers about your intentions
choice_c: It is easier to lock the wheels and cause a skid
choice_d: It wears out the brakes faster than braking on straight roads
explanation: The manual explains braking in a curve is dangerous because it is easier to lock the wheels and cause a skid; drivers should slow to a safe speed before entering the curve instead.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.3, Speed and Curves

question: The manual notes that posted truck and bus speed limits can be how much lower than car speed limits in some states?
explanation: The manual states that in many states, speed limits are lower for trucks and buses than for cars, and it can vary as much as 15 mph.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.5, Speed and Traffic Flow

question: On a downgrade, what does the manual say a driver must use as the principal way of controlling speed?
choice_a: Rapid gear shifting between neutral and drive
choice_b: The braking effect of the engine
explanation: The manual states you must use the braking effect of the engine as the principal way of controlling speed on downgrades, which is greatest near governed rpms in a lower gear.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.6, Speed on Downgrades

question: What does the manual identify as the number one cause of injury and death in roadway work zones?
explanation: The manual states speeding traffic is the number one cause of injury and death in roadway work zones.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.6.7, Roadway Work Zones

question: According to the 'one second per 10 feet' rule, how many seconds of following distance should a driver of a 40-foot vehicle leave at speeds below 40 mph?
explanation: The manual's rule of one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph means a 40-foot vehicle should leave four seconds of following distance.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.1, Space Ahead

question: For a 60-foot rig traveling at speeds greater than 40 mph, how many seconds of following distance does the manual recommend?
explanation: The manual states a 60-foot rig needs six seconds below 40 mph, and one additional second (seven seconds total) is added at speeds above 40 mph.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.1, Space Ahead

question: If you are being tailgated, what does the manual advise you should NOT do?
choice_a: Signal early and reduce speed gradually
choice_b: Avoid quick changes in speed or direction
explanation: The manual advises that if you are being tailgated, do not speed up, because it is safer to be tailgated at a low speed than a high speed.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.2, Space Behind (Dealing with Tailgaters Safely)

question: According to the manual, strong winds are usually a worse problem for which vehicles, and where can this problem be especially bad?
choice_c: Heavier vehicles, especially in open fields
choice_d: Lighter vehicles, especially coming out of tunnels
explanation: The manual states that the problem of strong winds making it difficult to stay in your lane is usually worse for lighter vehicles, and can be especially bad coming out of tunnels.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.3, Space to the Sides (Strong Winds)

question: Why can a loaded cargo van pass under a low bridge safely while the same van cannot when empty?
choice_a: Empty vans have larger tires that raise the vehicle
choice_b: Bridge clearances change based on vehicle weight sensors
choice_c: An empty van is higher than a loaded one
choice_d: Loaded vans compress their suspension and become taller
explanation: The manual explains the weight of a cargo van changes its height, and an empty van is higher than a loaded one, so clearing a bridge while loaded does not guarantee clearing it while empty.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.4, Space Overhead

question: What should a driver do before backing into an area, according to the space management section?
choice_b: Turn on the four-way flashers only
choice_c: Get out and check for overhanging objects such as trees, branches or electric wires
choice_d: Shift into the lowest forward gear
explanation: The manual advises getting out and checking for overhanging objects such as trees, branches or electric wires before backing into an area, since they are easy to miss while backing.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.4, Space Overhead

question: When making a right turn in a large vehicle that cannot complete the turn without swinging into another lane, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Come to a complete stop in the intersection before turning
choice_b: Turn wide to the left as you start the turn
choice_c: Back up slightly before completing the turn
choice_d: Turn wide as you complete the turn, keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb
explanation: The manual instructs turning wide as you complete the turn and keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb, which stops other drivers from passing on the right; turning wide to the left at the start is discouraged because a following driver may try to pass on the right.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.6, Space for Turns (Right Turns)

question: On a left turn, what should a driver make sure of before starting the turn?
choice_a: That all following traffic has stopped completely
choice_b: That the turn signal has been on for at least 30 seconds
choice_c: That the vehicle is in the leftmost lane available
choice_d: That the vehicle has reached the center of the intersection
explanation: The manual states that on a left turn, you must make sure you have reached the center of the intersection before you start the left turn, otherwise the left side of the vehicle may hit another vehicle due to off tracking.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.6, Space for Turns (Left Turns)

topic: Space to Cross or Enter Traffic
question: Why might a large commercial vehicle need a much larger gap to enter traffic than a car would?
choice_a: Because large vehicles have poorer brakes than cars
choice_b: Because of slow acceleration and the space large vehicles require
choice_c: Because large vehicles are legally required to wait longer
choice_d: Because large vehicles cannot use turn signals
explanation: The manual explains that because of slow acceleration and the space large vehicles require, a much larger gap may be needed to enter traffic than in a car.
source_note: Illinois Commercial Driver's License Guide (July 2025 edition, DSD CDL 10.30), Illinois Secretary of State -- Section 2.7.7, Space Needed to Cross or Enter Traffic
